name: AI News
blurb: Daily AI news from the publishers who broke it, split into headline coverage of the field and vendor announcements from the companies building it. Every story links to the original source, and any claim quoted in our coverage is cross-referenced against the laws, lawsuits, companies, tools, papers, and people already tracked in this atlas.

domains.name: AI Headline News
domains.blurb: The day's most consequential AI stories across law, policy, research, safety, and society, curated from 34 vetted feeds. Each item carries the original publisher link and a note on how it connects to the bills, cases, and frameworks tracked elsewhere on this site.

domains.name: AI Vendor News
domains.blurb: Product launches, model releases, pricing changes, and company announcements from the AI vendors themselves. Each item links to the vendor's original announcement and cross-references the company's profile in our AI Companies directory where one exists.

domains.name: This Week in AI
domains.blurb: A weekly record of what moved in AI policy and litigation, permalinked by ISO week.

domains.name: AI Historical Timeline
domains.blurb: From the 1940s to the present: Turing, the perceptron, expert systems, backpropagation, deep learning, AlexNet, transformers, and what followed.

reading.body:
The AI news archive tracks 338 pages of daily headlines and 14 weeks of policy coverage, drawn from 34 vetted sources and cross-linked to legal cases, legislation, and company profiles elsewhere on this site.

AI news cycles move faster than policy. The ratio of daily headlines to weekly policy summaries reflects the asymmetry: vendors announce products constantly, while laws take years to pass. This matters for infrastructure because regulation often lags the compute demands that new models create. A company can deploy a system requiring megawatts of power before the grid or regulators catch up.

The archive links claims back to original sources and to tracked entities in the atlas. This constraint does work: it prevents the site from amplifying unverified vendor claims or reporting policy moves that did not happen. It also means gaps are visible. The historical timeline currently has no pages, and vendor news has only one, suggesting coverage is weighted toward recent headlines rather than sustained analysis of how companies build or where they build.

What this data does not show is which stories connect to power, buildings, or compute constraints specifically. A reader interested in infrastructure must still click through to see whether a given news item describes a data center announcement, a grid bottleneck, or a regulatory action that would affect either one.
